Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) totally fun first (i.e., Entertainment game reappropriated), 
        (2) mostly fun first (i.e., design workshop with disabled stakeholders),
        (3) both fun and utility first (i.e., design workshop with diverse stakeholders), 
        (4) mostly utility first (i.e., primary utilitarian mechanic designed first),
        (5) totally utility first (i.e., made by clinicians or specialists, fun incorporated later)
reasoning: The work focuses on assistive technology, DIY-AT, and makerspaces as functional, utilitarian contexts (custom tools, clinical practice, co-designed engineer/clinician devices). It is an interview study about accessibility and barriers, not a game or entertainment system. Design motivations are primarily utility (access, assistive tech effectiveness), with any enjoyment or creativity of making as secondary. This aligns best with a mostly utility-first design rather than clinician-built only, so option 4 fits better than 5.

        (3) flexible structure with rules (i.e., improv),
        (4) flexible game (i.e., board game with house rules),
        (5) game with rigid rules (i.e., video game)
reasoning: The study is about makerspaces broadly defined as spaces where people come together to create things, including sewing circles and local yarn shops. Activities described involve open-ended making, hacking, and creating assistive or artistic projects rather than following predefined game-like rules or structures. This aligns best with unstructured play/making rather than any form of structured or rule-based game.

        (4) mostly chance-based (i.e., Uno),

reasoning: The study is a qualitative interview study about accessibility in makerspaces, not a game or contest. By the provided scale, this maps best to entirely skill-based.

        (1) entirely turn-based (i.e., tic tac toe),
        (2) follows a set of steps (i.e., viticulture's dynamic turn ordering),
        (3) turns are taken, but some actions can be taken at any time (i.e., pandemic),
        (4) most actions can be taken at any time, but there are some phases (i.e., PvP death reset timer),
        (5) entirely simultaneous (i.e., race)
reasoning: The study is qualitative interview research about makerspaces, not a game or structured turn-based system. There is no indication of ordered turns, steps, or phases; interactions in makerspaces and interviews occur in parallel and collaboratively, which best matches an entirely simultaneous structure among the given options.

        (1) entirely synchronous (i.e., real time strategy game),
        (2) mostly synchronous with a few asynchronous affordances (i.e., league of legends),
        (3) equal mix of synchronous and asynchronous affordances (i.e., helldivers 2),
        (4) mostly asynchronous with few synchronous affordances (i.e. cookie clicker),
        (5) entirely asynchronous (i.e., chess by postage mail)
reasoning: The paper is a qualitative interview study about makerspaces (physical and digital), not an interactive game or system with real-time coordination. Participation is via scheduled 45–75 minute semi-structured interviews and discussion of ongoing makerspace practices, which are inherently asynchronous interactions rather than synchronous gameplay or continuous real-time collaboration. Thus the studied design context is best characterized as entirely asynchronous.

Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely symmetrical (i.e., tic tac toe),
        (2) mostly symmetrical (i.e., undertale's differing NPC behaviors based on previous playthroughs),
        (3) both symmetrical and asymmetrical (i.e., pandemic with its similar turn structure but different character abilities),
        (4) mostly asymmetrical (i.e., tag),
        (5) entirely asymmetrical (i.e., keep talking, nobody explodes)
reasoning: The study is a qualitative interview study of two distinct participant types (makerspace operators vs disabled makers) with clearly different roles, perspectives, and forms of participation (e.g., operators providing space/support vs disabled makers creating/adapting AT for themselves and others). There is no shared, mirrored role structure like in a symmetric or mostly symmetric game; instead, interaction is framed around service, support, and differing responsibilities, which best maps to an entirely asymmetrical design.
